title: You take yourself along
hook: travel won't cure discontent, because you take yourself with you (Letters 28)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Calvisius Sabinus. Your line was nobody can learn it for me. Did the line you memorized come back without looking? Day four hundred fifty-seven.
screen: `CALVISIUS SABINUS — NOBODY CAN LEARN IT FOR ME.`

segments.voice: It's three in the afternoon on a gray Wednesday and you're scrolling flights. Somewhere warm. Somewhere with a different language and a different you, the one who's relaxed and reads novels and doesn't check email. Maybe you even go. And on the third night, in the lovely room by the sea, the same old worry turns up, like it had a ticket too. Lucilius has been traveling, hoping to shake off a heaviness he can't name. In the twenty-eighth letter, Seneca says he's not surprised it didn't work, and he explains why in one sentence. Today: you take yourself along.
screen: `SCROLLING FLIGHTS ON A GRAY WEDNESDAY.` → `THE WORRY HAD A TICKET TOO.` → `LUCILIUS TRAVELS, AND IT DOESN'T WORK.`

segments.voice: First, the diagnosis. Do you think you're the only one, Seneca asks, who has found that long trips and changes of scenery don't shake off sadness? You need to change your soul, not your sky. In Latin: animum debes mutare, non caelum. Second, Socrates. Seneca passes on a reply attributed to him, to someone who complained that travel did him no good: why are you surprised, when you take yourself along? The same cause that drove you out goes with you. Third, the cargo picture. Seneca says the trouble is like a heavy load that's badly stowed. Every lurch of the ship makes it worse. Run from place to place and you shake the load around. Set it down and the journey becomes a pleasure. Fourth, what he's not saying. He's not against travel. Once the soul is steadier, he says, any place is pleasant, and he adds a line that sounds very Stoic: I wasn't born for one corner; this whole world is my homeland. The change he's after isn't scenery. It's a habit, a judgment, a way of meeting the morning. Those come with you to the beach, and to the office, and they're the only luggage worth repacking.
screen: `CHANGE YOUR SOUL, NOT YOUR SKY.` · `SOCRATES: YOU TAKE YOURSELF ALONG.` · `A BADLY STOWED LOAD.` · `THE WHOLE WORLD IS MY HOMELAND.` · then, large: `A CHANGE OF SOUL.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've been hoping a change of place would fix: a new job, a move, a trip, a different chair. Hold it lightly. Then ask: what's the habit underneath it? Maybe rushing, or comparing, or never saying no. Name it in a few words. Now picture tomorrow morning in the same room you always wake up in, with that habit just slightly different. One small shift. Breathe there. The bell holds the time.
Socrates. His reply, passed on by Seneca: why are you surprised, when you take yourself along? Change the soul, not the sky. Today's word.
Your line: a change of soul. Today, change one habit, not one place: the small shift you pictured, tried once, right where you are. Day four hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: People who follow Seneca's advice often look for the habit behind a restless wish to be elsewhere, and work on that habit where they already are.

fork.setup: you've moved cities twice and the same restlessness keeps following you. what does the twenty-eighth letter suggest?
options: try a third city, farther away.
change your soul, not your sky.
fork.reveal: Seneca says the cause travels with you; the change has to be in the person, after which any place will do.

original.note: Latin, Seneca, Letters 28.1: you must change your soul, not your sky.

trapdoor: what you thought: a vacation will fix how I feel.
what it means: the same self goes on every trip; change the habit, and any place can be home.
what a scholar hears: Letters 28.1–4; Seneca quotes Virgil's 'lands and cities' line from Aeneid 3, and 28.4 states the Stoic cosmopolitan idea: patria mea totus hic mundus est.
recall: ask only what you'd ask openly

notes: Letters 28.1 'animum debes mutare, non caelum'; 28.2 Socrates' reply ('quid miraris... cum te circumferas?'); 28.3 the badly stowed cargo; 28.4 'non sum uni angulo natus, patria mea totus hic mundus est'. Confirm wording and numbering.
The Socrates saying is reported by Seneca; no earlier source is certain. Script says 'attributed to him'.
